newsitem.title: UK: UK funds bearish on US bonds, Japan stocks -poll.
newsitem.headline: UK funds bearish on US bonds, Japan stocks -poll.

text.p: UK-based fund managers are trimming their weightings in U.S. bonds and looking more closely at Europe against a background of strength in the U.S economy, a Reuter poll of fund managers showed.
And on the equity front Japan is being overshadowed by Asia, parts of Europe and Latin America, with opinions divided on the United States, the monthly Reuter poll of 15 fund managers said.
"For the start of January the big bets we are taking are with Europe," said Fergus Lynch, global strategist at Lehman Brothers.

"In the U.S. we recommend a significant underweight (in a global bond portfolio) because Europe will outperform...We are switching out of the UK and Denmark and into the long end in Germany and Belgium, and we are switching out of the U.S.."
Fund managers say they see better returns in Europe against a scenario of U.S. economic strength and the prospect of an interest rate rise. Europe they say represents better returns.
Allocations in U.S. bonds slipped to 30.4 percent this month from 33.1 in the last poll in December.
And some of the peripheral European bond markets have this month also lost out.
"We have cut Italy and Spain to neutral after being overweight for most of last year," said Matthew Merritt, global strategist at ING Barings.
"There is an awful lot of good news priced into Italian and Spanish bonds, including their likely participation in European monetary union and expectations of a smooth ride in."
The pace of growth in Germany as markets move into the second quarter could be the spanner in the works.
"If growth in Germany comes through, interest rate expectations will rise significantly, the Bundesbank will have to step up interest rates and that will hit the high yielders most," he said.
But Lynch disagreed on the outlook for the German economy.
"We don't see that there's going to be an economic recovery in Germany, and given the steepness of the German yield curve we feel the best place to be is at the long end."
On the equity front Japan in particular is losing out in the asset allocation stakes, with allocations slipping to 18.9 percent after 20.5 in December.
One global fund manager at a major investment house here said the likelihood of fiscal tightening, and the poor prospects for any major reforms, spelt a negative outlook.
"It will improve later in the year but sentiment is not good short term," he said.
Investors in U.S. equities were divided. The survey shows allocations there increasing slightly, to 28 percent from 25.2 but many fund managers were bearish.
"The near term risk is in the U.S. -- we see the market upside capped and moving into a valuation funnel," said ING Barings' Merritt.
But BZW was bullish on U.S. stocks.
"We may end up being the last bull left on Wall Street -- we probably had a higher weighting in Wall street than many," said Michael Hughes, head of economy and strategy at BZW.
The firm has increased its US equity weighting slightly.

"This is partly because I think it is the biggest emerging market in the sense that a lot of the emerging companies, the new technology companies, are centred mainly in America," he said, pointing to microchip, health, medicine and media firms.
But funds were otherwise divided on where the best returns lay, with some favouring parts of Asia and others Latin America and continental Europe.
"We are taking weightings from Japan and putting them in ex-Japan Asia," said one global fund manager.
He expected an end to Asia's cyclical downturn and an export-led recovery, particularly in the computer sector, with Singapore in particular set to benefit.
Both he and Merritt also saw growth in Europe ex-Britain.
"In continental Europe, the push for EMU is intact, and the low interest rate environment provides positive support," Merritt said.

The global fund manager said he was overweight in Germany, Scandanavia, Finland and Spain, and saw growth ahead in Latin America, with Argentina particularly in favour. --London newsroom +44 171 542 2734
